name: Deep state
scope: The belief, as its defining sources present it, that a hidden or semi-hidden network of unelected officials (above all military, intelligence and security bureaucrats, in some versions joined by financial, industrial or criminal interests) exercises power within the state independently of, and in opposition to, elected leaders and the formal political process. The sources (Merriam-Webster, EBSCO, Michaels, Fukuyama, Gingeras, Filkins) trace the term to Turkey's derin devlet and cover its American use. This profile covers the American strand that the sources name: the analytic or critical version of Lofgren, Peter Dale Scott and Glennon (a national-security and Wall Street 'state within a state' beyond democratic control) and the Trump-era version (Bongino, QAnon writers) in which the deep state works against an elected president. It takes the believers' own books (Lofgren, Scott, Steele, Bongino, White) as the ideology's own texts and the scholarship and journalism as its defining accounts. It leaves out the country-specific Turkish, Egyptian, Pakistani and other deep states as descriptions of regimes, the 'synarchy' and Masonic or antisemitic 'hidden hand' plot literature (such as the 1954 Hidden Government pamphlet, which names a different Master Plan), and critics' own views (Michaels, Fukuyama, Ingber, Cooper), who argue the US bureaucracy is not one.

summary: The deep-state idea holds that real power over national security and much else sits with a permanent network of unelected officials, in some versions joined by Wall Street, defence contractors or organised crime, which stays in place whoever wins elections and escapes the checks of the constitutional branches. Lofgren, Scott and Glennon present it as a critique of secrecy, surveillance, military-industrial and financial influence and money in politics; the Trump-era version applies the label to officials said to work against an elected president.

notes: Themes searched in Lofgren, Glennon and Scott's Dallas '63 and the Trump-era books: elections and money, surveillance, secrecy, foreign policy and bases, finance, courts and constitution, immigration, taxes. Lofgren's wider programme (infrastructure, tax, immigration, antitrust) is his own platform, not a tenet of the deep-state thesis, so it is left null. The critical strand and the Trump-era strand (Bongino, White) share only the claim of an unelected network; positions the strands do not share are null. Scott's Deep Politics and Iran-Contra books were searched for the same topics and settled none of the statements beyond what Lofgren and Glennon state.
